exam: How would you prioritize treatment for a patient with moderate depression and limited access to antidepressants? — Emphasise CBT as first‑line, outline steps, and note when medication is added.

A patient with HIV presents with low mood and poor ART adherence. Which psychosocial intervention is most appropriate and why? — CBT targeting health‑behaviour beliefs improves adherence without drug interactions.

During a trauma interview, the patient becomes tearful and avoids discussing the event. What is your next step? — Validate feelings, pause the session, and schedule a follow‑up focusing on safety and gradual exposure.

You are asked to run a CBT group in a district hospital with no psychologist. Who can deliver the therapy and what training is required? — Trained nurses or lay counsellors after a brief (2‑week) CBT workshop and supervision.

A patient reports hearing voices while also describing negative thoughts about self‑worth. How does this affect your CBT plan? — Presence of psychosis contraindicates standard CBT; refer for antipsychotic treatment and consider CBT‑p for psychosis.

Explain how you would adapt the cognitive restructuring technique for a patient who speaks only Swahili and uses the idiom ‘my heart is heavy’. — Translate the thought into local language, explore the meaning of ‘heavy heart’, and use culturally relevant metaphors for balanced thinking.

What are the key indicators that CBT is not working and you need to change strategy? — No reduction in PHQ‑9/GAD‑7 scores after 4‑6 sessions, persistent functional impairment, or emergence of safety concerns.

A community health worker asks whether CBT can replace medication for severe depression. How do you respond? — Clarify that CBT is first‑line for mild‑moderate cases; severe depression often needs combined pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy.
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: CBT is a structured, time‑limited psychotherapy that modifies maladaptive thoughts and behaviours. It is effective for common mental disorders and can be delivered with minimal resources.

b: Goal‑directed, usually 6‑12 weekly sessions
Therapist guides patient to identify and test unhelpful thoughts
Homework assignments reinforce learning
sections.p: CBT combines cognitive restructuring with behavioural experiments to reduce distress. It is evidence‑based for depression, anxiety, PTSD, and somatic symptom disorders, and can be adapted for low‑resource hospitals.

b: Automatic thoughts – rapid, often distorted cognitions
Core beliefs – deep‑seated assumptions about self, others, world
Behavioural experiments – planned actions to test beliefs
sections.p: The therapy rests on three pillars: automatic thoughts, core beliefs, and behavioural responses. Changing one influences the others, creating a positive feedback loop.

b: Improves medication adherence in HIV and TB
Reduces somatic complaints that mimic malaria or anemia
Provides a non‑pharmacological option when antidepressants are scarce
sections.p: In East African hospitals, CBT is used for depression linked to HIV, post‑malaria fatigue, and trauma after conflict or gender‑based violence. It can be delivered by nurses or lay counsellors after brief training.
When validated tools are unavailable, use locally adapted symptom checklists and clinical interview. Document baseline severity for monitoring.

t.b: Screen for depressive symptoms and severity; score ≥10 suggests moderate depression needing treatment
Screen for anxiety; score ≥10 indicates moderate anxiety suitable for CBT
Identify PTSD; score ≥33 warrants trauma‑focused CBT

b: Assessment – identify target problem, severity, and psychosocial stressors
Formulation – link thoughts, emotions, behaviours, and context
Skill teaching – cognitive restructuring, activity scheduling, relaxation
Homework – daily thought records, behavioural activation tasks
Review – evaluate progress, modify formulation, plan relapse prevention
sections.p: CBT follows a structured protocol: assessment, formulation, skill teaching, homework, and review. In low‑resource settings, group CBT or task‑shifting to trained lay workers is common.

b: First‑line for mild‑moderate depression when medication unavailable
Use of group format to maximise reach
Importance of cultural formulation – respect local idioms of distress
sections.p: Examiners expect you to describe CBT’s core steps, indicate when it is first‑line, and discuss adaptations for low‑resource environments.

b: Attempting CBT in active psychosis or severe mania – refer for specialist care
Skipping homework – reduces effectiveness
Using jargon – patients may not understand ‘cognitive distortions’
sections.p: Pitfalls include over‑medicalising normal grief, ignoring severe psychosis, and failing to adapt language to local concepts.
